lead.headline: Iran Fires on US Bases in Bahrain and Three Tankers Are Hit Near Hormuz, Setting Up a Tense Monday for Oil
lead.dek: The war's 268th day brought its widest weekend escalation in months, with Houthi missiles over Riyadh as well, just as markets arrive at Thanksgiving week in a correction.
body: The shipping war around the Strait of Hormuz escalated over the weekend. UKMTO reported two projectile strikes on outbound tankers early on Saturday 21 November, one about 20 km north and one about 31 km east of Khasab on Oman's Musandam peninsula, and Iran's navy said a third tanker caught fire after hitting a mine east of the strait. No casualties were reported. Iranian forces counted about 25 tanker incidents in the week to 21 November, according to Al Jazeera.

Later on Saturday Iran launched drones and ballistic missiles at US facilities in Bahrain, home of the US Fifth Fleet. Bahrain said it intercepted several attacks and that a fire broke out at a civilian industrial site without injuries; Iranian claims of hits on air-defence batteries were not confirmed. Deputy Foreign Minister Gharibabadi called the US blockade an act of war and Foreign Minister Araghchi said it must be broken. More than 14 Iranian tankers are reported waiting off Kharg Island, but no sailing was confirmed by Sunday morning, and a 'Khat Shekan' (line-breaker) tanker signal that appeared in the Gulf on 22 November was a spoof, according to TankerTrackers.

The pressure also reached Saudi Arabia from the south: the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh on 21 November and another fired toward western Saudi Arabia early on 22 November, after its strikes on Hodeidah port. The Houthis have threatened Jeddah and all Saudi Red Sea ports, the outlet for crude diverted from Hormuz via the East-West pipeline. Saudi Arabia's Tadawul, which trades on Sundays, is the first big market to price the weekend.

Oil goes into this with momentum pointing the other way. Brent settled at $92.57 on Friday 20 November, down 3.4% on the week for a third weekly loss and about 21% below its 30 October close of $117.64, as analysts at Julius Baer pointed to robust Middle East exports and an IEA-forecast surplus of about 2m barrels a day. Saxo Bank's Ole Hansen said further falls may be hard without evidence of a resolution. Diplomacy continues: a Qatari delegation held talks in Tehran on Friday, and President Trump has said he is in no hurry to decide on wider strikes.

impact.title: What it means for markets
points: Brent's Monday open is the first price on the Bahrain strikes and the weekend tanker attacks; Friday's $92.57 settle reflected surplus worries, not this escalation.
Gulf tanker war-risk premiums and freight rates stay elevated, and Saudi Red Sea ports now sit inside the Houthi threat zone.
Gulf equities (Tadawul on Sunday, Bahrain and Dubai) are the most exposed; Treasuries and the dollar are the havens that worked on Friday.
A real convoy breakout from Kharg would put Iranian barrels back into a market priced for their absence, which would weigh on crude rather than lift it.

body: The shipping war around the Strait of Hormuz intensified over the weekend. UKMTO reported two separate projectile strikes on tankers leaving the Gulf early on Saturday 21 November: one vessel was hit at the stern about 20 km north of Khasab on Oman's Musandam peninsula, and another in its engine room about 31 km east of the town. Iran's navy separately said a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine in a restricted area east of the strait, saying the ship had switched off its identification systems; it was unclear whether that vessel was one of the two UKMTO cases. Iranian state media called the night's operations its most intense yet, and Iran insists ships coordinate with its forces and use Iranian-designated lanes.

The conflict also widened onshore. Iranian media said two waves of drones and ballistic missiles targeted US facilities in Bahrain on Saturday, naming Sheikh Isa air base and the Juffair naval facility that hosts the US Fifth Fleet; the Guards claimed hits on Patriot batteries and a radar, which neither Bahrain nor the US confirmed. Bahrain said it intercepted several attacks, reported a fire at a civilian industrial compound with no injuries, and asked the UN Security Council to enforce Resolution 2817. CENTCOM denied an Iranian claim that a US F-16 was damaged on Friday evening.

On the blockade, more than 14 Iranian tankers are reported to be waiting off Kharg Island. Gharibabadi called the US blockade an act of war and said Tehran had told Washington the convoy would head to China, while Foreign Minister Araghchi said the blockade must be broken and that reopening the strait would be easy if the US ended the blockade, lifted sanctions and acknowledged past mistakes. On Sunday 22 November a ship signal calling itself 'Khat Shekan' ('line-breaker') appeared moving in the Gulf, but TankerTrackers said satellite imagery showed no such vessel and the transmission borrowed another tanker's call sign. Iranian officials have still not confirmed a sailing.

Diplomacy continues in parallel. A Qatari delegation held about two hours of talks in Tehran on Friday evening, and President Trump told Fox News he wants a 'permanent' deal that stops Iran obtaining nuclear weapons and was never seeking regime change. He has said he is in no hurry to decide on wider strikes.

For oil, the weekend's incidents land on a market that has been sliding. Brent settled at $92.57 on Friday 20 November, up 0.6% on the day but down 3.4% on the week, its third straight weekly fall, and about 21% below the 30 October close of $117.64. Bloomberg-reported analysts at Julius Baer and Global Risk Management said supply and surplus forecasts are outweighing geopolitics, while Saxo Bank's Ole Hansen said further falls may be hard without evidence of a resolution.

read.title: The Ledger's Read
paragraphs: The weekend did not give markets the calm they needed. Wall Street closed Friday in correction after a seventh straight loss, with the S&P 500 at 6,914.90 and the VIX near 36, and the trigger was governance at the market's largest AI company rather than earnings. Over Saturday and Sunday the newsflow shifted from Silicon Valley to the Gulf: three tankers hit around Hormuz, Iranian strikes on US facilities in Bahrain, and Houthi missiles over Riyadh. Oil had spent three weeks pricing out war risk on surplus forecasts, so Monday's open is the first test of whether that complacency holds.

Policy makers are already leaning against the equity slide in Asia. Taiwan's short-sale curbs and state-fund buying are classic stabilisation tools, but they rarely change direction on their own; what matters more is whether this week's AI-hardware reports, Dell above all, show that orders are holding up. In rates, the Treasury's $183bn of note sales will show whether Friday's haven bid has depth, while widening CCC spreads say the stress is moving from stocks into the weakest credits, including AI-infrastructure borrowers.

The week is short and dense. Watch the euro-zone flash PMIs and Kalshi's New York hearing on Monday, Dell on Tuesday, and PCE, GDP and durable goods on Wednesday before Thanksgiving thins liquidity. Outside the big markets, frontier currencies from Nairobi to Lagos to Buenos Aires are under strain, with Nigeria's central bank and Brazil's spending vote as early catalysts, and Spain votes on 29 November.

stories.headline: Wall Street Enters a Holiday-Shortened Week in Correction, With Dell, PCE and $183 Billion of Note Sales Ahead
stories.summary: US stocks start Thanksgiving week after a seventh straight loss: the S&P 500 closed Friday 20 November at 6,914.90 (-3.64%), the Nasdaq Composite at 22,682.49 (-5.01%) and the Dow at 48,216.66 (-1.79%), with the S&P and Dow more than 10% below their peaks and the VIX at 35.89. Nvidia lost about 23% over the week, its worst since October 2008, and the Nasdaq about 10%. The calendar is crowded before Thursday's holiday: HPE and Zoom report on Monday, Dell, Workday and HP Inc. on Tuesday, and October PCE inflation, Q3 GDP and durable goods land on Wednesday. Markets close on Thursday and stocks shut early on Friday.
stories.market: Friday's after-hours bounce of 1.5%-3.6% in Nvidia, AMD and QQQ will be tested at Monday's open; thin holiday liquidity can amplify moves either way after a week when tech funds took in $12.3bn just before the slide.

body: The S&P 500 fell 260.93 points on Friday 20 November to 6,914.90, its seventh straight decline, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1,196.71 points to 22,682.49 and the Dow 880.40 points to 48,216.66. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF closed about 11.5% below its 6 October record, putting the benchmark in correction territory alongside the Dow, and the VIX rose 7.45 points to 35.89, its highest close since April 2025.

The trigger was a reported widening of the SEC's civil investigation of Nvidia into accounting questions, which sent the stock down 14.01% to $125.53 on Friday and about 23% over the week. Reports on 21 November said investigators have not identified specific statements and that the inquiry is at an early stage. Chips, AI-infrastructure names and crypto fell together, while Treasuries rallied and defensive staples and health insurers rose.

Positioning makes the week ahead delicate. LSEG Lipper data showed global equity funds took in $59.23bn in the week to 18 November, the most since mid-June, including $12.3bn into technology funds, so many recent buyers are under water. US spot bitcoin ETFs lost $1.25bn over 16-20 November.

The week's tests come quickly: HPE, Zoom and Agilent after Monday's close; Dell, Workday, Autodesk and HP Inc. on Tuesday, with Dell carrying a $95bn AI-server backlog into its report; and on Wednesday October PCE inflation, Q3 GDP and durable goods, the last big inflation print before the 9 December Fed decision. US markets are shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving and stocks close early on Friday.

body: European stocks ended the week of 16-20 November with their heaviest losses since March. The DAX gave up 2.60% on Friday to 24,801.22 and 7.29% over five sessions, while London's FTSE 100 held up best with a 5.10% weekly fall. Italy's FTSE MIB fell 2.48% to 48,703.73 and Spain's IBEX 1.63% to 18,873.09 on Friday.

The sell-off was led by the same AI and chip names that hit Wall Street and Asia, with semiconductor-equipment makers among the biggest losers. Bonds rallied: the German 10-year yield fell 8.8bp over the week to 3.302%.

The week ahead opens with the November flash PMIs on Monday, the first survey evidence on whether market turmoil and German metalworker strikes are denting activity. Volkswagen and IG Metall open in-house pay talks in Emden on Tuesday 24 November, and Bayer has its first Frankfurt session since a US judge approved its $7.25bn Roundup settlement.

Weekend geopolitics cut both ways for Europe: Iran's strikes on US facilities in Bahrain raise energy risk, while Zelensky's acceptance of US-proposed talks with Russia before Christmas is the first sign of new diplomacy in weeks. NATO allies discuss Russia's missile incursion into Poland in Brussels on Monday.

stories.summary: Indian stocks were the exception in last week's global rout: the Sensex closed Friday 20 November up 1.08% at 83,919.71 and the Nifty 50 up 1.12% at 25,800.60, both nine-month highs and a fourth straight weekly gain (+2.85% and +2.61%). Foreign investors have bought a record $12.21bn of Indian shares in November as of 20 Nov as funds rotate out of chip-heavy Asian markets. The rupee closed at 93.32 per dollar. This week brings the close of Coal India's Mahanadi Coalfields sale on Monday and the Crystal Crop listing on 26 Nov.
stories.market: Bank and financial stocks led the rotation (bank index +5.9% on the week); weekend Gulf escalation is the main risk for an oil-importing market, since Brent feeds directly into the rupee and inflation.

body: India closed the week of 16-20 November near its highs while most of Asia slumped. The Sensex rose 897.96 points on Friday to 83,919.71 and the Nifty 50 286.30 points to 25,800.60, even though GIFT Nifty had pointed to a gap-down open near 25,315.50.

The driver has been money moving out of AI-heavy markets such as Taiwan and Korea. Foreign buying reached a record $12.21bn for November as of 20 November, and Indian bank shares gained 5.9% over the week.

Two risks stand out for the week ahead: the weekend escalation around Hormuz and Bahrain, which matters for an oil importer whose currency sits near 93 per dollar, and whether the global sell-off resumes strongly enough to pull flows back. In the primary market, Coal India's Mahanadi Coalfields offer for sale closes on Monday 23 November, with grey-market quotes pointing to a flat debut.

Policy makers reacted over the weekend. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said on 21 November that from 23 November short sales will be barred in any stock that closed lower the session before, and raised the minimum short-sale margin to 150% from 130%. Premier Cho Jung-tai told the National Financial Stabilization Fund to step up purchases.

In Korea, Seoul Economic Daily reported on 22 November that Hana Securities sees room for the Kospi to fall to 4,300 and BNK puts a worst case at 4,500. Foreigners sold a net 168 trillion won of Korean shares from May through November, the paper said.
In Japan, the Nikkei fell 5.1% on Friday as SoftBank slid; Tokyo core CPI on Friday 27 November (forecast 3.0%) is the week's main data for the Bank of Japan.

stories.headline: Treasuries Carry a 4.92% 10-Year Yield Into $183 Billion of Note Sales and the Last PCE Before the Fed
stories.summary: The 10-year Treasury yield fell 12bp to 4.92% on Friday 20 November, closing below 5% for the first time since 10 November, as the 2-year dropped 13bp to 4.63% and the 30-year 9bp to 5.31%. The haven bid now meets heavy supply: the Treasury sells $177bn of bills and $69bn of 2-year notes on Monday 23 November, part of $183bn of 2-, 5- and 7-year notes this week. Below investment grade the stress is building, with CCC spreads at 13.61 percentage points on 19 November after a 45bp weekly widening. October PCE inflation on Wednesday is the last major price print before the 9 December Fed decision.
stories.market: Auction demand will show whether Friday's flight to safety has staying power; the 2s10s curve stood at 29bp, and wider junk spreads hit AI-infrastructure borrowers such as CoreWeave.

body: Government bonds were the one broad asset class that worked in last week's sell-off. On Friday the 10-year yield fell 12bp to 4.92%, the 5-year 15bp to 4.71% and the 2-year 13bp to 4.63%, leaving the 2s10s spread at 29bp. The TLT long-bond fund rose 1.37% as gold, copper and bitcoin fell.

Supply is the near-term test. Monday 23 November brings $177bn of bills and a $69bn 2-year note sale, and 5- and 7-year notes follow before the holiday, for $183bn of coupon supply in a shortened week.

Credit markets are flashing more strain than Treasuries. An analysis published on 22 November put the CCC spread at 13.61 percentage points on 19 November after a 45bp widening in a week, a move seen in only six of 151 comparable periods, while BB and BBB spreads widened only 24bp and 6bp. Global high-yield funds lost $1.36bn in the week to 18 November, per LSEG Lipper.
On Wednesday, October PCE inflation, the second estimate of Q3 GDP and durable goods arrive together; futures priced about a 90% chance of a 25bp Fed hike in December as of Friday.

stories.summary: Futures priced about a 90% chance of a 25bp Fed hike at the 9 December meeting as of Friday 20 November, down from higher odds earlier in the week, after Governor Lisa Cook said delay risks leaving the Fed behind the curve and Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson backed further deliberate increases. The policy range is 3.75%-4.00%. Wednesday's October PCE release (core forecast +0.3% m/m) and Q3 GDP (+3.4% estimate) are the week's decisive data.
stories.market: A hot PCE print would push 2-year yields back up after Friday's 13bp fall; a soft one would revive the half-point-hike unwind and help rate-sensitive sectors.

body: Markets ended the week of 16-20 November still expecting the Fed to raise rates in December. Futures priced roughly a 90% probability of a 25bp increase from the 3.75%-4.00% range, about 56% for a further move by January and an implied peak near 4.47%, as of Friday.

Fed officials have not wavered publicly. Governor Lisa Cook, speaking in Chile on 20 November, defended her October vote for a hike and warned against falling behind the curve; Philadelphia's Anna Paulson said she favours deliberate increases and is open to back-to-back moves, without endorsing a half-point step.

The data this week will test that. October PCE inflation and Q3 GDP arrive on Wednesday 25 November at 14:30 CET, a day before Thanksgiving, with the November jobs report on 4 December the last major release before the 8-9 December meeting.

Silver fell about 7% during Friday's session. Gold had been sold alongside chips and crypto as investors raised cash and markets priced a December Fed hike, rather than acting as a haven. body: Gold's slide accelerated on Friday 20 November. Spot touched $3,513.54 in the US morning, and COMEX December futures later settled at $3,515.40, down 4.62%, according to Xinhua. The metal fell about 8% over the week, its biggest weekly decline since March, and is more than a third below its January highs.

The selling came as investors liquidated across assets during the AI rout and as futures priced about a 90% chance of a December Fed hike, which raises the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding metal.

Silver fell harder, with the SLV fund down 6.74% on Friday. The week ahead brings PCE inflation on Wednesday, and the weekend's Iranian strikes on US facilities in Bahrain will show whether geopolitical demand can stabilise prices.

stories.headline: Iran War, Day 268: Three Tankers Hit Near Hormuz and Bahrain Bases Targeted as Tehran Says the Blockade 'Must Be Broken'
stories.summary: UKMTO said two outbound tankers were struck by projectiles early on 21 November, one about 20 km north and one about 31 km east of Khasab, while Iran's navy said a third tanker hit a mine east of the strait after ignoring warnings; no casualties were reported. Iranian armed forces counted about 25 tanker incidents in the week to 21 November, roughly three a day, according to Al Jazeera's Tehran correspondent. Late on 21 November Iran launched drones and missiles at US facilities in Bahrain, which said it intercepted several attacks and that a fire broke out at a civilian industrial site without injuries. Deputy Foreign Minister Gharibabadi called the US blockade an act of war and said Washington had been told a tanker convoy would sail for China, but no departure from Kharg has been confirmed and a vessel signal billed as a blockade-runner on 22 November was a spoof, according to TankerTrackers. Brent settled at $92.57 on Friday, down 3.4% for a third weekly loss.
stories.market: Brent (BZ=F) closed the week at $92.57 (-3.4% w/w) as traders weighed tanker attacks against record Hormuz flows cited by the US Energy Secretary and an IEA-forecast surplus; Monday's open will price the Bahrain strikes and any convoy move. War-risk premiums for Gulf tankers and Gulf equities (Bahrain, Saudi Tadawul) are the most exposed.

body: The shipping war around the Strait of Hormuz intensified over the weekend. UKMTO reported two separate projectile strikes on tankers leaving the Gulf early on Saturday 21 November: one vessel was hit at the stern about 20 km north of Khasab on Oman's Musandam peninsula, and another in its engine room about 31 km east of the town. Iran's navy separately said a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine in a restricted area east of the strait, saying the ship had switched off its identification systems; it was unclear whether that vessel was one of the two UKMTO cases. Iranian state media called the night's operations its most intense yet, and Iran insists ships coordinate with its forces and use Iranian-designated lanes.

The conflict also widened onshore. Iranian media said two waves of drones and ballistic missiles targeted US facilities in Bahrain on Saturday, naming Sheikh Isa air base and the Juffair naval facility that hosts the US Fifth Fleet; the Guards claimed hits on Patriot batteries and a radar, which neither Bahrain nor the US confirmed. Bahrain said it intercepted several attacks, reported a fire at a civilian industrial compound with no injuries, and asked the UN Security Council to enforce Resolution 2817. CENTCOM denied an Iranian claim that a US F-16 was damaged on Friday evening.

On the blockade, more than 14 Iranian tankers are reported to be waiting off Kharg Island. Gharibabadi called the US blockade an act of war and said Tehran had told Washington the convoy would head to China, while Foreign Minister Araghchi said the blockade must be broken and that reopening the strait would be easy if the US ended the blockade, lifted sanctions and acknowledged past mistakes. On Sunday 22 November a ship signal calling itself 'Khat Shekan' ('line-breaker') appeared moving in the Gulf, but TankerTrackers said satellite imagery showed no such vessel and the transmission borrowed another tanker's call sign. Iranian officials have still not confirmed a sailing.

Diplomacy continues in parallel. A Qatari delegation held about two hours of talks in Tehran on Friday evening, and President Trump told Fox News he wants a 'permanent' deal that stops Iran obtaining nuclear weapons and was never seeking regime change. He has said he is in no hurry to decide on wider strikes.

For oil, the weekend's incidents land on a market that has been sliding. Brent settled at $92.57 on Friday 20 November, up 0.6% on the day but down 3.4% on the week, its third straight weekly fall, and about 21% below the 30 October close of $117.64. Bloomberg-reported analysts at Julius Baer and Global Risk Management said supply and surplus forecasts are outweighing geopolitics, while Saxo Bank's Ole Hansen said further falls may be hard without evidence of a resolution.

stories.headline: Houthis Fire Ballistic Missiles at Riyadh and Western Saudi Arabia After Coalition Hits Hodeidah Port
stories.summary: The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted three Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Riyadh early on 21 November, the third straight day of air alerts in the capital, and later destroyed a drone headed for the kingdom's south. Shortly after 01:40 Riyadh time on 22 November it said it destroyed another ballistic missile fired toward western Saudi Arabia following a civil-defence alert for the Mecca region. The barrage follows the coalition's 20 November 'special operation' on Hodeidah port and Sanaa; the Houthis say coalition strikes killed 41 people in 24 hours, a figure AFP could not verify. The Houthis have threatened Jeddah and all Saudi Red Sea ports and told airlines Saudi airspace is unsafe, though no strike on those ports has been reported.
stories.market: The threat to Jeddah and Yanbu puts Saudi Red Sea export and import capacity, which carries crude diverted from Hormuz via the East-West pipeline, in play, supporting Brent and Red Sea war-risk premiums. Saudi equities and the PIF-linked financial district are directly exposed.

body: The Saudi-Houthi war moved further into the kingdom over the weekend. The coalition backing Yemen's government said it intercepted three ballistic missiles fired at Riyadh early on Saturday 21 November; an AFP journalist heard two explosions as authorities warned of an aerial threat, and the alert was later lifted. It was the third consecutive day of alerts in the capital, after a Houthi strike on 19 November damaged the Public Investment Fund's tower in the King Abdullah Financial District.

Late on Saturday, Saudi civil defence issued an alert for the Mecca region, and the coalition said at about 01:42 local time on Sunday 22 November that it had destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward western Saudi Arabia. No Houthi claim had surfaced by Sunday morning; the group has previously denied targeting Mecca and named East-West pipeline pump stations and Yanbu oil facilities as targets. Alerts on Saturday also covered Najran, Al-Sulayyil and Jazan.

The escalation follows the coalition's 20 November operation against Hodeidah port, which spokesman Turki al-Malki said hit facilities used to bring in weapons and missiles, and strikes in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz. The Houthis said 41 people were killed in 24 hours, while government forces said 193 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded; AFP could not verify either figure. Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree told workers and residents near Jeddah and other Saudi Red Sea ports to evacuate and urged shipping lines to remove vessels.

On the ground, government forces reported air strikes north of Marib and clashes in al-Jawf and Lahj on 21 November. The UN said fighting could threaten aid routes and that more than 350,000 people have been displaced. Pakistan's foreign minister condemned the attack on Riyadh's financial district.

stories.headline: Four More Killed in Gaza as Lebanon's President Demands Full Israeli Withdrawal
stories.summary: Gaza's civil defence said Israeli fire killed four people on 21 November, three in a drone strike on a vehicle carrying food in Gaza City's Tel al-Hawa and one in Jabalia; the Israeli military said it struck militants. That follows four deaths near Bureij on 20 November, and the health ministry says more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire. In Lebanon, President Joseph Aoun used his independence-day eve address on 21 November to demand that Israel withdraw from all Lebanese territory and that Hezbollah hand its weapons to the state, as Israeli strikes hit the Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun districts. Lebanon counts at least 4,386 killed since the war resumed on 2 March 2026.
stories.market: Little direct oil impact, but the strains keep Israeli risk premia and Lebanese Eurobonds sensitive to whether the June 2026 Lebanon framework and the Gaza truce hold. Israeli shekel and defence names react more to the Iran front.

body: Violence continued inside Gaza's ceasefire lines over the weekend. The civil defence agency said three people died when an Israeli drone hit a vehicle carrying food for displaced people in Tel al-Hawa, Gaza City, on Saturday 21 November, and one man was killed by gunfire in Jabalia al-Balad. The Israeli military said it struck several operatives in the area. A day earlier, four men were killed southwest of Bureij camp in central Gaza, in what the army said was a strike on Hamas fighters.

The truce that took effect in October 2025 is increasingly hollow. The health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable, says more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since it began; Israel says seven soldiers and a contractor have died. Earlier in the week Israel ran its first ground push beyond the Yellow Line since the ceasefire, and the Board of Peace warned the Security Council that the truce could collapse.

In Lebanon, President Joseph Aoun marked the eve of the 83rd independence anniversary by demanding Israel leave 'every inch' of Lebanese territory, stop attacks and return detainees, while criticising interference by parts of Iran's government and pledging to bring all weapons under state control. Implementation of a US-mediated framework signed in June 2026 has stalled, with Hezbollah refusing to disarm and Israel continuing strikes.

Israeli strikes were reported on 21 November in the Nabatieh, Bint Jbeil and Marjayoun districts, according to Lebanon's National News Agency. The health ministry says at least 4,386 people have been killed in Lebanon since 2 March 2026, and 8,953 since October 2023.

stories.headline: Missile Strike on Zelensky's Hometown and a 275-Drone Raid on Russia Follow a Night of Kyiv Grid Attacks
stories.summary: Two ballistic missiles hit central Kryvyi Rih late on 20 November, killing two people and injuring about 60, and officials said follow-up strikes hit rescuers. Ukraine's air force counted three ballistic missiles and 148 drones overnight into 21 November, after 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones the night before. Russia's defence ministry said it downed 275 Ukrainian drones over 12 regions overnight, with explosions reported near the Baltic oil port of Ust-Luga, and Reuters industry sources say Russian refinery runs are down about 45% since late October. NATO's Rutte condemned Friday's incursion of Russian missiles and a drone into Poland, while Zelensky said on 21 November he doubted Putin was ready to compromise.
stories.market: Dutch TTF gas closed Friday at €89.54/MWh after a 6% jump on cold, a Norwegian outage and the grid strikes; EU storage below 70% leaves it sensitive to any wider escalation. Ukrainian drone hits on Russian refining and Baltic ports support European diesel cracks, while European defence stocks stay bid on NATO-airspace incidents.

body: Russia kept up its air campaign after the 19-20 November mass strike on Kyiv. Late on 20 November two ballistic missiles hit a restaurant car park in central Kryvyi Rih, President Zelensky's hometown; a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic were killed and about 60 people sought treatment. City head Oleksandr Vilkul said further missiles and drones struck as emergency crews arrived. Zelensky said Russia is using more repeat strikes on rescue sites.

Ukraine's air force recorded three ballistic missiles and 148 drones overnight into 21 November, with hits at 19 locations, after the previous night's 84 cruise missiles and 404 drones. An attack on a DTEK facility on 20 November cut power to 41,000 households in Odesa region, and Ukrenergo kept scheduled outages in place across parts of the country on 21 November. Ukraine's energy ministry says Russia has carried out more than 1,000 strikes on the energy sector since September, and the EU Council has approved nearly €8bn for infrastructure repairs.

Ukraine's long-range campaign continued. Russia's defence ministry said it destroyed 275 Ukrainian drones between the evenings of 20 and 21 November across 12 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea; the Leningrad governor reported 61 over his region and explosions were reported near Ust-Luga, one of Russia's biggest oil and product export terminals, without confirmed damage. Earlier in the week drones hit a crude pumping station in Tatarstan and the Ilsky refinery, and the main road span of the Kerch Bridge remains down. Reuters industry sources put the drop in Russian refinery processing at about 45% since late October, and several Russian regions have imposed fuel-sale limits.

The war is spilling over NATO's edge. Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in southeastern Poland on 20 November; Prime Minister Tusk called it a deliberate provocation and NATO Secretary-General Rutte on 21 November condemned the violation and pledged to defend Polish territory. Estonia will close all five road crossings with Russia from 1 December, and Denmark expelled Russia's defence attaché.

On diplomacy, Trump said after meeting Putin in China that the Russian leader wants a negotiated end, but Zelensky said on 21 November he was less convinced. Moscow still demands Ukraine's withdrawal from all of Donbas, which Kyiv rejects; US security guarantees for Ukraine remain under negotiation.

stories.headline: Kordofan Monitors Report Civilian Deaths as Sudan's Army Pushes Past Abu Zabad and the RSF Presses on Blue Nile
stories.summary: The Kordofan Human Rights Observatory said on 21 November that RSF fighters killed three civilians near Abu Qalb in West Kordofan on 20-21 November, a claim not independently verified, and that at least 17 civilians died in the area during the week, including in air and drone strikes, with about 3,000 displaced. An army special-forces spokesman said troops broke through RSF positions northeast of Abu Zabad. In Blue Nile, the RSF-SPLM-N alliance's 19 November claim to have taken Bau, about 60 km from Damazin, still stands, and Sudan's authorities say the army is mobilising there. Prediction market Polymarket put the chance of a ceasefire by 31 December at 8% as of 21 November.
stories.market: Sudan's war matters mainly through gold, the main hard-currency source for both sides, and regional trade with Egypt, Ethiopia and the Red Sea. COMEX gold fell 4.6% to $3,515.40 on Friday on Fed-hike expectations, a global rather than Sudanese driver.

body: Fighting in West Kordofan is taking a growing civilian toll as the army advances. The Kordofan Human Rights Observatory said on 21 November that RSF fighters killed three civilians around Abu Qalb and Al-Shanabla on 20-21 November and looted cattle; the claim has not been independently verified, and the Dar Hamar Emergency Room has made similar accusations.

The same observatory said at least 17 civilians were killed in the Abu Qalb area during the week and around 3,000 people displaced. It blamed an army drone strike on 15 November for 15 deaths, while other groups gave tolls of 13 and nine; the operator of a 17 November drone strike on a school sheltering displaced families in Ghubeish has not been established. Army special-operations spokesman Mohamed Didan said troops dismantled RSF defences northeast of Abu Zabad.

On the southeastern front, the RSF and its SPLM-N ally claimed on 19 November to have captured the Bau locality headquarters, about 60 km southwest of Damazin, the Blue Nile capital and home of the army's Fourth Infantry Division. Sudanese authorities say the army retains the initiative and is mobilising troops. About 11.4 million people are forcibly displaced across Sudan.

For markets, the link is gold, which funds both sides, and trade routes to Egypt, Ethiopia and Port Sudan. December gold futures settled at $3,515.40 an ounce on 20 November, down 4.62% on the day, as expectations of a Fed rate hike firmed; the war itself is not moving global prices.

stories.headline: Burnham and Brussels Sign Food, Carbon and Youth Deals, but University Fees Hold Them Up
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and EU leaders signed agreements at a Brussels summit on 20 Nov creating a common food-safety area, linking the UK and EU carbon markets from 2028 and opening a youth mobility scheme capped at 100,000 people a year per side. Britain estimates the food deal could add up to £5.1bn a year to its economy and the carbon link up to £3.8bn, but the package is on hold until a dispute over EU students' tuition fees is settled within six months. On 21 Nov the Conservatives claimed the carbon link would add £281 a year to household costs, a figure the government called completely wrong.
stories.market: The carbon link would exempt about £6.5bn of UK exports such as steel from the EU's border carbon levy, a plus for steelmakers and food exporters; Reuters used a rate of $1 = 0.7630 pounds (about $1.31) on 20 Nov.

body: The summit in Brussels produced three agreements. A sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) area would remove certificates and checks on trade in animals, plants and related food products from March 2028, in return for the UK keeping outcomes consistent with EU rules. UK food, drink and feed exports to the EU fell 26% in value between 2019 and 2025, according to a House of Lords paper.

The UK and EU emissions trading systems are to be linked from 2028, letting allowances count for compliance in either market and exempting goods such as steel from each side's carbon border levy. The EU's levy took effect in January 2026, and the UK's own version starts on 1 January 2027.

Young people aged 18 to 31 would be able to live and work or study on the other side for up to three years, with the scheme running by January 2030. The cap of 100,000 per side per year is double the UK's initial offer.

The deals are on hold until the two sides agree on fees for EU students, which Brussels wants set at domestic levels; the Russell Group says that would cost UK universities £570m. Car market access under the EU's Made in Europe rules also remains open. The government plans to introduce a Cutting Costs Bill in Parliament later this week.

stories.summary: Crystal Crop Protection's ₹455.49 crore IPO finished 17.68 times subscribed when bidding closed on 20 Nov, according to InvestorGain, yet its grey-market premium stood at ₹14.5 at 10:02 IST on 22 Nov, implying a debut near ₹286.5, about 5.3% over the ₹272 top of the band. The premium has slid from ₹40 on 13 Nov. Coal India's offer for sale in Mahanadi Coalfields, which closes on Monday 23 Nov, carried a premium of just ₹1 (0.51%) at 08:02 IST on 22 Nov per IPO Market, with another tracker showing zero; allotment is due on 25 Nov and a tentative listing on 27 Nov. SME issue Watrana Rentals held a ₹65 premium (26.5%) ahead of its own close on Monday. Two mainboard issues open next week: Foodlink F&B Holdings (26-30 Nov), quoted at a ₹12 premium by IPO Watch, and Integris Medtech (27 Nov-1 Dec).
stories.market: Premiums point to a modest Crystal Crop listing on 26 Nov and a flat start for Mahanadi Coalfields, a gauge of appetite for India's public-sector stake sales; grey-market quotes are unofficial and not endorsed by SEBI or the exchanges.

body: Demand for Crystal Crop Protection's shares did not translate into a rising grey-market price. InvestorGain records the issue as 17.68 times subscribed, yet the unofficial premium fell over most of the ten sessions it tracked, from ₹40 on 13 Nov to about ₹14-14.5 by Sunday morning. IPO Watch showed ₹14, or an estimated listing near ₹286. The stock is scheduled to list on 26 Nov.

Mahanadi Coalfields, a pure offer for sale by Coal India, enters its final day on Monday 23 Nov with grey-market traders signalling little or no listing gain: IPO Market showed ₹1 over the ₹136 upper price, while IPO Watch showed nil. ETV Bharat earlier reported day-one subscription of 0.38 times, with institutions at 1.26 times and retail at 0.13 times. Allotment is due on 25 Nov and listing, tentatively, on 27 Nov.

Next week's pipeline is led by Foodlink F&B Holdings, whose book-built issue combines a ₹192 crore fresh issue with an offer for sale of 88.35 lakh shares and runs from 26 to 30 Nov, with listing tentatively on 3 Dec. Integris Medtech follows with a ₹600 crore fresh issue plus an offer for sale of 1.08 crore shares from 27 Nov to 1 Dec. Neither had fixed a price band as of 21 Nov, per ETV Bharat. Among small issues, Shree Siddhivinayak Greentech (₹130-142) opens on 25 Nov with no premium quoted.

stories.headline: Customs Agents Seize Nearly 10.5 kg of Smuggled Gold in Hyderabad and Dhaka on the Same Day
stories.summary: India's Directorate of Revenue Intelligence seized 2.98 kg of 24-carat gold in 25 bars, valued at about ₹3.83 crore, from a hidden compartment behind the tail lamp of an SUV travelling from Kolkata to Hyderabad on Saturday 21 Nov, and arrested two people, the Free Press Journal reported. The metal and vehicle were seized under the Customs Act and the DRI says it is investigating the wider network. In Dhaka on the same morning, Bangladesh's Airport Armed Police Battalion detained three men leaving Hazrat Shahjalal airport with 7.5 kg of gold paste worth Tk 11.67 crore, The Business Standard (Bangladesh) reported. Police allege the three belong to an organised ring bringing gold from Saudi Arabia; the claims have not been tested in court.
stories.market: Smuggled bullion bypasses import duties and official import data in two of the world's big jewellery markets; the scale of individual seizures in the multi-crore range shows how strongly informal channels still compete with formal imports.

stories.headline: Taiwan Bans Short Selling of Any Falling Stock and Orders the State Fund to Buy More
stories.summary: Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said on 21 Nov that from Monday 23 Nov short selling will be barred in any stock that fell in the previous session, its first blanket restriction of this kind since 2015, and it raised the minimum short-sale margin to 150% from 130%. Premier Cho Jung-tai met economic and financial agency heads the same morning and told the NT$500bn (US$15.18bn) National Financial Stabilization Fund to step up its buying. The Cabinet called the slide temporary and raised its 2026 growth forecast to 12%.
stories.market: The Taiex reopens on 23 Nov from 36,033.29, its lowest close in nearly seven months after a 6.23% fall on 20 Nov; Friday's intraday low left it 28.48% below its 6 Oct record of 49,968.92. TSMC and other chip names are the main test, and the central bank was told to watch the New Taiwan dollar closely.

body: Taiwan's regulators went further over the weekend after the Taiex's worst week since 1991. The Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) said on Saturday 21 Nov that, from Monday 23 Nov, investors may not short any stock that ended the previous session lower. Only two days earlier it had applied that ban only to stocks that had fallen 3.5% or more.

The FSC also raised the minimum margin for short sales to 150% from 130%, so short sellers must post more collateral. It stopped taking new applications from brokers to issue put warrants, asked lenders to suspend securities lending and to recall lent shares early or not renew them, and said it would keep pressing listed companies to buy back their own shares.

Premier Cho Jung-tai met economic and financial agency heads on Saturday morning and told them to step up stabilisation work. He asked the NT$500bn National Financial Stabilization Fund, which has been cleared to intervene since 6 Nov, to buy more. The finance ministry was told to provide more financing and credit guarantees to businesses, and the central bank to watch the currency market and the New Taiwan dollar closely.

Officials played down the slide. The finance ministry said it mostly reflected heavy losses abroad, not structural problems at home. The economics ministry pointed to strong AI-infrastructure spending: October revenue at electronics distributors rose 92.2% from a year earlier and at chipmakers 63.6%. The Cabinet said the economy grew 14.22% in the first three quarters, and it now expects 12% growth for 2026, up from 11.05% in August.

The index closed at 36,033.29 on 20 Nov after falling 2,393.60 points, or 6.23%, the third-largest one-day point drop on record. Whether the broader short ban and more state buying can slow the selling will become clear when trading resumes on Monday.

stories.headline: Amazon Nears a $7.5 Billion Deal for Chip-Switching AI Start-Up Decart, FT Says
stories.summary: Amazon is in advanced talks to buy San Francisco AI start-up Decart in a deal valuing it at about $7.5bn, the Financial Times reported on Saturday 21 Nov, adding that an agreement could be announced as soon as this week but that talks could still fall apart. Decart's main software lets developers move AI workloads between different chips, and it was an early user of Amazon's Trainium3 processors, an alternative to Nvidia GPUs. The price would nearly double the $4bn valuation from a $300m funding round in May whose backers included Sequoia Capital and Nvidia. Israeli outlet Calcalist reported on 18 Nov a price above $7bn, rising to about $7.5bn with earnouts, paid in cash, stock and deferred payments. Neither company has confirmed a deal.
stories.market: For Amazon (AMZN) the price is small relative to its size, but the deal would strengthen AWS's push to win AI workloads away from Nvidia (NVDA) hardware. Oppenheimer lifted its AMZN target to $310 from $285 on 19-20 Nov.

body: The Financial Times said on Saturday that Amazon's talks with Decart had reached their final stages and could produce a signed agreement early this week, though the discussions could still collapse. The Wall Street Journal had reported in October that the two were discussing a deal worth nearly $7bn.

Decart was founded in 2023 by three Israeli engineers, Moshe Shalev and brothers Dean and Orian Leitersdorf. Its core product helps developers switch AI models between chip types, an increasingly valuable skill as companies try to reduce dependence on a single supplier. It is also building real-time video and interactive 'world' models called Lucy and Oasis.
The start-up was an early adopter of Trainium3, the in-house chip Amazon launched last year to compete with Nvidia's GPUs, which gives the deal an obvious fit with AWS's cloud strategy.
Israeli press reports from 18-19 Nov described a mix of cash, stock and deferred payments, with founders staying for five years. None of these terms has been confirmed by either company.

body: Dell is the headline tech report in a holiday-shortened week. stories.headline: Kalshi faces Monday hearing on a New York restraining order it says could shut its exchange nationwide
stories.summary: New York state Justice Melissa Crane will hear Attorney General Letitia James's request for a temporary restraining order against prediction-market operator Kalshi on Monday 23 November, after two federal judges declined last week to keep the case out of state court. The order would bar Kalshi from offering sports contracts without a state gaming licence and, as drafted, from operating within or from New York, where the company is headquartered. Kalshi argued in a letter to the court that the relief is unprecedented and would effectively shut a federally regulated exchange for customers everywhere; it says 1.2 million New Yorkers use its service and that it is open to a deal with the state. The underlying suit seeks up to $36 billion in restitution and penalties, a claim that stands even if the restraining order is denied, according to reports on 21 November.
stories.market: A nationwide halt would hit a platform valued at $22 billion with about $178 billion in annualised volume (per reports on 21 Nov 2026), and would shift the competitive picture for licensed sportsbooks DraftKings (DKNG) and Flutter (FLUT) before US markets reopen on Monday.

body: The fight over who regulates US prediction markets moves to a Manhattan state courtroom on Monday. Attorney General Letitia James sued KalshiEX in July, alleging that its sports event contracts amount to unlicensed gambling under New York law; her complaint also targets trading by users aged 18 to 20 and contracts tied to New York college teams.

Kalshi tried to move the case to federal court, where it argues that its contracts are derivatives under the exclusive oversight of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. US District Judge Vernon Broderick sent the case back to state court on 19 November. On 20 November Judge Lorna Schofield, at an emergency telephone hearing, refused the CFTC's request to stop the state judge from ruling, which cleared the way for James to renew her request for a restraining order.

The key question for Monday is reach. Because Kalshi is based in New York City, an order barring it from operating 'from' the state could, the company says, halt trading for every customer. Gaming-law attorney Daniel Wallach told Yahoo Finance he expects at least New York users to be restricted, with a ruling possible within days or weeks. Commentary on the draft order's headquarters language has also raised the question of whether other New York-based platforms could be caught.

The case is one front in a wider conflict. The CFTC has sued 12 states to assert federal jurisdiction, and three of four federal appeals courts that have ruled so far have sided with states. Separately, the CFTC ordered Kalshi on 17 November to remove markets on what President Trump might say in speeches, and earlier this month opened an inquiry into whether Kalshi improperly self-certified contracts.

stories.headline: Bayer's approved Roundup deal still waits on appeals before payments start

Payouts are due in capped annual instalments over up to 21 years, designed to decline over time, and the timing of the first payments remains open. Bayer shares rose 1.2% to 55.16 euros on Friday, a move the report ties to a product launch rather than the ruling, which came after European markets had closed. Berenberg raised its price target to 62 euros from 53.50 euros on 17 November and kept a Hold rating. Bayer still denies that glyphosate causes cancer.

stories.headline: Tariff refunds reach Walmart, Apple and FedEx as shoppers and importers fight over the rest
stories.summary: Publicly traded US companies expect or have already received $28.5 billion in refunds of tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down in February, according to a ProPublica tally cited by Forbes on 20 November. FedEx expects $3.3 billion, Walmart $2.9 billion and Apple $2.2 billion; at least nine firms plan to use part of their refunds for staff bonuses, and none has said it will refund customers. Consumers have filed class actions against retailers including Walmart, Target and Nike seeking a share. In a separate class case at the Court of International Trade covering more than 330,000 importers that paid an estimated $166 billion, the Justice Department must respond to a request for a relief order by 9 December.
stories.market: Refunds are a one-off boost to earnings and cash for FedEx (FDX), Walmart (WMT) and Apple (AAPL), while consumer suits add a litigation question for retailers such as Target (TGT) and Nike (NKE).

body: The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in February in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorise the tariffs, but left the question of refunds to the Court of International Trade.

Customs opened a refund portal in April, and by 2 October had sent about $126 billion in refunds and interest to the Treasury for payment. About three-quarters of the $166 billion collected under the IEEPA tariffs has now gone back to importers, according to Forbes.

Judge Richard Eaton ruled in March that all importers of record are entitled to refunds; the government appealed to the Federal Circuit in June, and the order is on hold for importers that did not sue. On 8 October the court certified a class in Freestyle World v. United States covering importers that paid between 1 February 2025 and 19 February 2026, and class lawyers sought a relief order on 10 November.
Shoppers will only benefit if companies choose to pass refunds on, which is why consumer class actions have targeted big retailers.

stories.headline: SEC proposes taking direct control of the Consolidated Audit Trail
stories.summary: The Securities and Exchange Commission proposed on Friday 20 November to take over the Consolidated Audit Trail, the market-wide surveillance database now run by a FINRA-overseen entity and funded by the industry. Under the plan, exchanges and broker-dealers would report trade data to the SEC or its designee, and the system's costs would depend on annual appropriations from Congress. SEC officials put current operating costs at about $137 million a year, down roughly 45% since 2024. The SEC chair said the change would bring accountable governance and cost discipline; market operators warn it could leave the system exposed to government shutdowns. The proposal opens a 60-day public comment period.
stories.market: The shift would change who pays for and governs a system that exchanges such as Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), Nasdaq (NDAQ) and Cboe (CBOE) and their broker-dealer members have funded, with implications for their regulatory costs.

body: The Consolidated Audit Trail records order and trade activity across US equity and options markets so regulators can reconstruct events such as sudden crashes. It has been operated by an organisation overseen by FINRA and paid for by exchanges and broker-dealers.

The SEC's proposal of 20 November would make the agency itself, or a designee, the recipient of that data. Funding would move to the annual congressional budget process, which critics in the industry say could put surveillance at risk during a government shutdown.

The plan follows an earlier 2026 decision to stop the systematic collection and storage of traders' personal details, such as names, addresses and dates of birth, in the database. The SEC will decide whether to adopt a final rule after the 60-day comment period.

stories.headline: SEC scrutiny of Nvidia widens to its accounting as Huang's congressional interviews near
stories.summary: The SEC's civil investigation of Nvidia now includes potential accounting issues, Reuters reported on Friday 20 November, widening a probe first reported by the Wall Street Journal on 17 November into whether the company's disclosures misled investors. Reports on 21 November said investigators have not identified specific statements or transactions, though attention has fallen on Nvidia's change last year to reporting revenue by customer headquarters, which removed Singapore from its geographic breakdown; the New York Times said the inquiry is at an early stage and may not lead to charges. Neither Nvidia nor the SEC commented. Nvidia shares closed down 14.01% at $125.53 on 20 November. Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney and Garry Tan have signed a letter urging the board to reinstate former CEO Jensen Huang, which the board has said it will not do. An investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing.
stories.market: Nvidia (NVDA) lost about 23% in the week to 20 November, its worst week since October 2008, and roughly $1 trillion in market value since Huang's exit (per Motley Fool and TNW, 21 Nov 2026); the probe keeps pressure on chip stocks when US trading resumes on Monday.

body: The new element is the accounting angle. Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, reported on 20 November that SEC enforcement staff are scrutinising possible accounting issues at Nvidia, beyond the disclosure questions the Wall Street Journal reported on 17 November. Neither outlet could say which issues are under review.

Coverage on 21 November pointed to Nvidia's switch to booking revenue by customer headquarters rather than billing address, which ended its separate Singapore line. The Financial Times had reported that revenue booked through Singapore had risen 70% to $104 billion when that disclosure stopped, according to TNW. Nvidia has also said its quarterly 10-Q filing will be delayed into the coming weeks while an independent board committee completes a review, per Business Today.

The governance fight continues alongside. Board chair Harvey Jones has said the board does not intend to reinstate Huang, who resigned on 12 November, while President Trump and a group of technology figures including Musk, Sweeney and Tan have urged his return. Law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz is examining the circumstances of his departure.

Other probes remain open: the Justice and Commerce departments are separately investigating whether Megaspeed diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China, California's attorney general served a subpoena on 19 November, and House Democrats are asking whether Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's family, influenced the government response; Cantor called the claims inaccurate.

stories.summary: Argentina's informal 'blue' dollar was quoted at ARS 1,655 to buy and ARS 1,675 to sell in El Cronista's Saturday 21 Nov survey, a record that leaves it up ARS 110 in November and ARS 145 since the start of 2026. Banco Nación's official retail rate was ARS 1,600 to sell, a gap of about 4.7%, while the MEP and CCL financial rates stood at ARS 1,677.81 and ARS 1,788.44. In Nigeria, the official NFEM rate closed Friday 20 Nov at ₦1,394 per dollar, a loss of more than ₦13 on the day, Tribune reported; street dealers were quoted at ₦1,466 to buy and ₦1,482.50 to sell on 21 Nov by OsunDefender. Iran's open-market dollar was quoted at 269,250 tomans (about 2.69 million rials) at 17:49 Tehran time on 21 Nov by Arzparz, little changed on the day.

The naira's official-street gap has widened to roughly 6% from about 2% at end-October as offshore investors trim exposure, WithinNigeria reported.

stories.headline: A 'Line-Breaker' Tanker Tests the US Blockade on Paper, but Trackers Say the Ship Does Not Exist
stories.summary: A vessel broadcasting the name 'Khat Shekan', loosely 'line-breaker', appeared on MarineTraffic early on Sunday 22 Nov moving at 8.5 knots in the Persian Gulf, and was widely read as an Iranian test of the US naval blockade, The Week reported. Its AIS signal carried an Iranian maritime identity, but its call sign matched a Liberian-flagged tanker in US records, and its stated destination was an oil terminal that MarineTraffic linked to Nigeria. TankerTrackers said the tanker does not exist, that satellite imagery showed no ship making those moves and that the listed arrival time implied an Iran-to-Nigeria voyage of a few hours. The signal followed Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's remark on Friday that the blockade must be broken, made in response to reports that Iran was loading oil for export; Iranian officials have not confirmed any convoy. On 20 Nov the US Treasury said no Iranian oil was on the water outside the blockade and none had been loaded since Operation Economic Outcast began.
stories.market: A real breakout would put Iranian barrels back into a market priced for their absence, while a spoofed signal underlines how sanctions evasion now leans on falsified ship identities; oil traders and tanker insurers are watching Kharg Island loadings for confirmation either way.

body: The 'Khat Shekan' signal surfaced in the early hours of Sunday 22 Nov, when ship-tracking service MarineTraffic showed a vessel of that name under way at 8.5 knots inside the Persian Gulf. The transponder data listed an Iranian maritime identification number, but the call sign belonged, according to US records, to the Liberian-flagged tanker Stolt Bobcat, and the destination field read only 'OIL TERMINAL', which MarineTraffic matched to a Nigerian terminal.

Vessel-tracking firm TankerTrackers rejected the sighting outright. Its founder said the tanker does not exist and that satellite imagery showed no ship making the reported movements; the firm also pointed out that the estimated arrival time would have required crossing from Iran to Nigeria within hours, a sign of a spoofed signal. It added that Iran was unlikely to send out a very large crude carrier given how many have come under fire in recent months.

The episode lands amid reports that Tehran wants to gather tankers at Kharg Island, the hub of its crude exports, and break the blockade. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told the ILNA news agency on Friday 20 Nov that the blockade must be broken. Iranian officials have not confirmed that any convoy is moving, and The Week said the source gave no export volumes.

Washington's position is that Iran's seaborne trade has stopped. In its 20 Nov release designating four alleged Iranian 'oil trustees', Treasury said there was no Iranian oil on the water outside the military blockade and that none had been loaded since Operation Economic Outcast began; Secretary Scott Bessent said Iran had exhausted its seaborne oil and might never recover money for oil it had already sold.

Spoofed and borrowed identities are a long-running feature of the so-called shadow fleet. When Treasury and the State Department sanctioned 22 tankers on 8 Oct, gCaptain reported that the ships flew more than a dozen flags and that TankerTrackers counted 173 Iran-linked tankers still outside US sanctions.

stories.headline: Chainflip Freezes Its Exchange After a $4.86 Million Vault Drain; Cyber's Bridge Hit by Unauthorised Minting
stories.summary: Cross-chain swap protocol Chainflip put itself into full safe mode on Saturday 21 Nov, halting deposits, withdrawals, swaps and quoting, after an attacker drained about $4.86 million from its Ethereum vault at roughly 02:10 ET, The Block reported. The haul, 520.2 ETH, 3.25 million USDC and 758,000 USDT, was converted to about 2,909 ETH and pushed into the Tornado Cash mixer in 38 batches within minutes, too fast for stablecoin issuers to freeze, according to Coinpedia and The Block. Security firms say the theft used a valid signature from the validators' shared signing key rather than a code bug; Chainflip has not confirmed the cause. The FLIP token fell about 34%, cutting its market value from about $41.6 million to $27.1 million. Separately, about 5.2 million CYBER tokens were minted without authorisation on Solana on 21 Nov in a suspected $1 million bridge exploit, prompting Upbit and Bithumb to suspend CYBER deposits and withdrawals.
stories.market: FLIP lost about a third of its value and CYBER dipped about 8% to $0.2024 before recovering to about $0.213; the incidents keep pressure on cross-chain bridges and swap venues already under scrutiny as conduits for stolen crypto.

body: Chainflip said on 21 Nov it was aware of a potential exploit affecting its vaults and moved the protocol into full safe mode as a precaution. The withdrawal from its Ethereum vault took under ten minutes, and blockchain-security firm AMLBot traced nearly all of the proceeds into Tornado Cash. Vaults on Bitcoin and Solana appeared unaffected, The Block said.

Analysts' early findings point to a compromised signing key rather than a flaw in the smart contract. Chainflip's vault key is held jointly by 150 validators, needs 100 signatures and rotates every three days, last on 18 Nov. Bitquery found the malicious transaction carried a transaction number wildly out of sequence with the protocol's roughly 300,000 earlier signatures, suggesting it was produced outside Chainflip's normal system. Chainflip has not said how the key was compromised or whether victims will be repaid.

COINOTAG reported on 22 Nov that Chainflip offered the attacker a 10% bounty, expiring on 23 Nov, to return the funds as a white-hat recovery. In September the protocol lost about $736,000 in a separate incident; validators later voted to reimburse affected liquidity providers from surplus funds.

In the Cyber case, 5,213,000 CYBER were minted on Solana at 11:13 ET on 21 Nov, and the same amount left the Ethereum contract securing the token's LayerZero bridge two minutes later, Coin Edition reported. Most tokens were sold for ETH, and 575.29 ETH moved to a new address. Cyber, formerly CyberConnect, said it was investigating and urged users to avoid its bridge and token migrations.

stories.headline: Ransomware Gang Puts Nvidia on Its Leak Site; Chipmaker Points to a Third-Party Partner
stories.summary: Ransomware group The Gentlemen listed Nvidia on its dark-web extortion portal on 18 Nov, claiming to have stolen sensitive data and threatening to publish it unless the company negotiates, VARINDIA reported on 21 Nov; a countdown on the site reportedly runs to 28 Nov. The group has not published evidence that it reached Nvidia's internal systems. Nvidia said it was investigating a potential incident involving a third-party partner and had found no indication that its own networks were compromised. The Gentlemen operates a ransomware-as-a-service model and claims more than 1,000 victims. The case follows extortion group n0n's claim of a vendor leak affecting JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard customer marketing data, reported by The Wall Street Journal on 19 Nov.
stories.market: Both incidents point to supplier networks as the weak link for large listed companies; JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard all said payment systems and card data were not affected, and no regulator action has been reported.

body: The Gentlemen added Nvidia to its leak portal on 18 Nov and, according to VARINDIA, set a ten-day deadline that expires on 28 Nov. It says it holds sensitive company information but has offered no public proof. Nvidia's response framed the matter as a possible incident at an outside partner, saying it had seen nothing to suggest its own networks were breached.

In the earlier card-network case, extortion group n0n posted its claims on 16 Nov, according to Reuters as cited by Fox News, and The Wall Street Journal reported the leak on 19 Nov. JPMorgan said attackers appear to have accessed marketing data held by vendors, possibly including some customer names and email addresses, and plans to offer free credit monitoring; Reuters reported more than 16,000 customer email addresses, a figure it could not verify. Mastercard said a small group of cardholders in one benefit programme had email addresses exposed, and Visa said no card numbers were affected and that a provider in Asia-Pacific was involved.
Investigators have not established whether a single provider sits behind all three card-industry exposures, and no link has been reported between that case and the Nvidia claim.

stories.headline: Ecuador Arrests a Cuban Fugitive Wanted in the US Since 2012 Over an Alleged Florida Staged-Crash Insurance Fraud
stories.summary: Ecuadorian police and the US Marshals Service arrested Abel de Jesús Pérez Camuza, a 57-year-old Cuban national, in Guayaquil on Friday 20 Nov, Interior Minister John Reimberg announced on 21 Nov, according to CiberCuba. He has faced US federal charges since March 2012 of conspiracy to commit postal fraud, healthcare fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Prosecutors allege a scheme run through two rehabilitation clinics in Cape Coral, Florida, that recruited people to stage traffic accidents and file false insurance claims, with investigators documenting more than 200 acts of postal and medical fraud and estimated takings of up to $22.5 million a year. He was handed to Ecuador's migration authorities to continue his expulsion to the United States. Each count carries up to 20 years in prison; he has not been convicted.

stories.headline: Private Credit's Exit Queue: Big BDCs Fill as Little as 38% of Redemption Requests as a $300 Billion PE Debt Wall Looms
stories.summary: Investors in the largest non-traded private-credit funds are still being paid out only in part, according to tender data compiled by Real Investment Advice on 20 Nov: Blackstone's BCRED bought back about 90 million of roughly 181 million shares tendered in its third-quarter offer, a 49.9% fill worth $2.13 billion, while Ares Strategic Income Fund filled about 38.2% of requests. Requests at Blue Owl's two biggest non-traded credit funds eased to $4.2 billion in the third quarter from $5.4 billion in the first, with each fund buying back the 5% quarterly cap. In a Fortune commentary on 21 Nov, finance professor Derek Horstmeyer, citing The Wall Street Journal, said private-equity-backed companies face a debt wall of about $300 billion, much of it due in 2028-29, and that a record 30% of buyout holdings have been held six years or more, per PitchBook. Houlihan Lokey data reported on 19 Nov showed the size-weighted private-credit default rate rising to 1.5% from 0.8%.
stories.market: Blue Owl Capital Corp. (OBDC), the listed BDC, closed at $10.97 on 13 Nov against a $14.32 net asset value at 30 Sept, about 77 cents on the dollar, signalling the discount public markets apply to private loan marks; the 4.34% expense ratio on WisdomTree's private-credit ETF (HYIN) illustrates the cost hurdle for retail products.

body: Quarterly tender results show the gap between what investors want back and what semi-liquid private-credit funds will pay. At Blue Owl Credit Income Corp., requests equalled 16.8% of shares in the third quarter, down from 21.9% in the first, while at Blue Owl Technology Income Corp. they stayed near 39%; both funds repurchased the 5% maximum. Seven of ten non-traded BDCs tracked by Crowdfunded Wealth prorated their latest offers, filling between 12.8% and 49.9% of requests. KKR's FS Income Trust Select was an exception, paying all of its 5.06% requests.

Fortune's 21 Nov commentary argues the industry is turning to retail and retirement savers for exits: private credit and private equity are moving into ETFs, mutual funds, perpetual vehicles and 401(k) plans, backed by the White House. Horstmeyer warns about fees, opaque valuations and what AQR's Cliff Asness calls 'volatility laundering', the understating of risk in assets that rarely trade, and notes a nine-year backlog of unsold private-equity assets cited by the WSJ.

Credit quality is also slipping at the margins. Houlihan Lokey data reported by Alternative Credit Investor on 19 Nov showed defaults by borrower count rising to 3.7% from 2.5%, reaching 3.9% among borrowers with less than $100 million of EBITDA, and 15.1% of borrowers with interest coverage below 1.0 times. At a Senate Banking hearing on 19 Nov, SEC nominees said private credit does not pose a financial-stability risk.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike-Zscaler: Founder's Backing Seen as Key as Jefferies Puts a 'Reasonable' Takeout at $255
stories.summary: A day after Bloomberg and Reuters reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy Zscaler, Reuters said on 21 Nov that any deal would probably need the support of founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry, Zscaler's largest shareholder. Jefferies said in a note updated on 21 Nov that a combination has significant merit and called $255 a share a reasonable takeout price, about 31% above Zscaler's regular-session close of $194.82 on 20 Nov. It put the odds of a deal at $255 or more at better than a coin flip, while flagging possible regulatory scrutiny and the need for a willing seller. Reuters put Zscaler's market value at about $32bn and said its shares rose as much as 17% after hours on Friday, while CrowdStrike fell about 8%. Neither company has commented, and the talks could still end without an agreement.
stories.market: ZS closed down 5.3% in Friday's regular session before the report, so even a 17% after-hours gain leaves it below the $255 Jefferies figure; CRWD's after-hours drop reflects concern about the cost to the buyer. Palo Alto Networks (PANW), the main listed rival, saw BMO and BTIG set targets of $425 and $442 in the two days to 21 Nov.

body: The weekend brought no confirmation from either company, but it did shift attention to who would need to agree. Reuters, citing two people familiar with the matter, reported on 21 Nov that a transaction would likely need the backing of Jay Chaudhry, who founded Zscaler in 2007, runs it and is its largest shareholder.

Jefferies, in a note dated 21 Nov in TipRanks' metadata, said the deal has significant merit. It argued that Zscaler's network traffic data would strengthen CrowdStrike's AI position and take it into network security, making it a tougher rival to Palo Alto Networks in several product lines. The broker called $255 a share a reasonable takeout price and said a deal at that level or above was more likely than not, while warning that the size of the combination could draw antitrust attention.

The $255 figure is about 31% above Zscaler's regular-session close of $194.82 on Friday 20 Nov, which was down 5.3% on the day as the Nasdaq slid. After the reports, the stock rose as much as 17% after hours, per Reuters, while CrowdStrike fell as much as about 8%.
Zscaler shares had dropped about 25% from their late-October closing high of $260.45 before the report. Reuters put Zscaler's market value at about $32bn as of Friday's close.

stories.headline: Wonder Sounds Out Walmart, Target and Kroger on a Sale of Grubhub
stories.summary: Marc Lore's food-hall company Wonder is exploring a sale of Grubhub, and its bankers have approached Walmart, Target, Kroger and other retailers to gauge interest, the Wall Street Journal reported on 20 Nov; the talks are described as preliminary and no price was disclosed. Wonder bought Grubhub in 2024 for $150m in cash plus about $500m of assumed debt, and in September sold Grubhub's college-campus delivery business to DoorDash for $300m, alongside a $125m DoorDash investment in Wonder. Grubhub has lost market share and active customers, and Amazon replaced its Prime delivery tie-up with Grubhub with an Uber Eats arrangement. Wonder is separately preparing for a possible IPO and has made a preliminary regulatory filing.

stories.headline: AI Listings Lose Momentum: DayOne Shelves a $5 Billion IPO as Anthropic Enters Week Two Near Its Offer Price
stories.summary: Singapore data-centre operator DayOne has paused plans for a US IPO of up to $5bn that had been targeted for as early as this quarter, Bloomberg reported on 20 Nov, citing investor worry about AI valuations and volatility; it may still list in 2027 or opt for a smaller deal. The news came as Anthropic ended its second session at $88.91, down 8.5% and only about 7% above its $83 IPO price, after an intraday low of $83.05. Bloomberg's weekend coverage on 21 Nov framed the slide as a test of whether anything can revive the AI trade. Anthropic's next scheduled events are entry into the MSCI global standard large-cap index on 1 Dec and its first lock-up release, of up to 303m shares, on 15 Dec.
stories.market: The pause underlines how the selloff in AI-linked stocks is closing the new-issue window: DayOne's underwriters include Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citigroup. For ANT, index-fund buying from 30 Nov-1 Dec and possible Nasdaq-100 entry later in December are potential demand offsets to lock-up supply.

body: DayOne, which runs hyperscale data centres in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia and counts TikTok owner ByteDance as its biggest customer, filed for a US listing in October. Bloomberg reported on 20 Nov that it has put the plan on hold and is weighing a delay or a smaller offering; no final decision has been made.

Its retreat follows other signs of strain in the issuance calendar: Danish drugmaker Leo Pharma was reported on 6 Nov to be considering pushing its Copenhagen IPO into 2027, citing market turmoil and a narrow window before Thanksgiving.

Anthropic's own record deal remains the benchmark. The stock closed its second session on 20 Nov at $88.91, on volume of about 400.5m shares, giving a market value of about $1.16tn based on listed shares, per the Motley Fool. It traded between $83.05 and $92.56, and has fallen about 23% from its $115.10 intraday peak on debut day.

Upcoming supply and demand dates are now in focus. MSCI has confirmed the shares join its global standard large-cap index from 1 Dec, with the change effective after the close on 30 Nov. A Nasdaq-100 fast entry is estimated before the open on 21 Dec but not yet confirmed. Lock-up releases of up to 303m shares each are due on 15 Dec and 5 Jan, and up to 353m shares each on 19 Jan and 2 Feb.
detail.consensus: Early broker targets of $105-$150 sit well above the $88.91 price, but no new target changes were reported over the weekend.

stories.headline: Junk-Bond Stress Builds at the Bottom as CCC Spreads Jump and $183 Billion of Treasury Notes Loom
stories.summary: The spread on CCC-rated US junk bonds reached 13.61 percentage points over Treasuries on Thursday 19 Nov, having widened 45bp in the week, a move seen in only six of 151 comparable periods, according to an analysis published on 22 Nov. BB and BBB spreads widened a more modest 24bp and 6bp. CoreWeave's bonds due 2031 traded at a spread of 1,062bp on 19 Nov, a level usually associated with distress. Global high-yield bond funds lost $1.36bn in the week to 18 Nov, including $2.31bn from US funds, per LSEG Lipper. The Treasury will sell $177bn of bills and $69bn of 2-year notes on Monday 23 Nov, part of $183bn of 2-, 5- and 7-year notes this week.
stories.market: Stress is concentrated in the weakest credits and AI-infrastructure borrowers, while the 10-year Treasury yield fell about 12bp on Friday as investors bought safety. Wells Fargo set a $115 target on CoreWeave (CRWV) in the two days to 21 Nov.

body: The selloff in AI stocks is now showing up in the riskiest corners of credit. CCC-rated spreads hit 13.61 percentage points on 19 Nov after a 45bp weekly widening, while BB spreads widened 24bp and BBB spreads 6bp, showing that the damage is concentrated at the bottom of the ratings scale.

Vanguard has noted that four of more than 150 CCC issuers account for over 30% of CCC spreads, with telecoms and media the most strained. CoreWeave, a heavy borrower to build AI data centres, had its 2031 bonds trade at a 1,062bp spread on 19 Nov; one of its co-founders has bought back some of the debt.

Investors pulled $1.36bn from global high-yield funds and $2.78bn from dollar-denominated bond funds in the week to 18 Nov, per LSEG Lipper, while euro-denominated bond funds took in $2.34bn, the most since 12 Aug.

Government supply is heavy before Thanksgiving: $177bn of bills and $69bn of 2-year notes on Monday, and $183bn across 2-, 5- and 7-year notes for the week, all settling on 30 Nov. That is $58bn more gross coupon settlement than the 16 Nov refunding.

stories.headline: Brokers Turn to Defensives: TD Cowen Upgrades UnitedHealth and Humana, Eight Firms Lift Walmart Targets
stories.summary: TD Cowen's Ryan Langston upgraded UnitedHealth and Humana to Buy from Hold on 20 Nov, raising targets to $455 from $402 and to $485 from $430, and naming UnitedHealth his best idea for 2027 with a path to mid-to-high-teens EPS growth through 2028. The calls came after insurers sold off on 18 Nov when CMS proposed tougher audits of Medicare Advantage payments; both stocks rose in Friday pre-market trading despite the broader selloff. Walmart targets also rose after its results: TD Cowen to $147 from $125, DA Davidson to $145 from $132, Bernstein to $142, BofA to $141, BTIG to $140, Piper Sandler to $138, and Morgan Stanley and Mizuho to $135. Walmart's US comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%.
stories.market: UNH and HUM traded higher before Friday's open against a falling market as investors looked for defensive names; the CMS audit proposal stays open for comment until 19 Jan 2027, keeping policy risk alive for managed-care stocks.

body: TD Cowen's double upgrade of the two biggest Medicare Advantage insurers was the most notable rating change of a volatile Friday. Langston expects better benefit design in Medicare Advantage, a recovery at Optum Health and firmer Commercial and Medicaid margins to drive UnitedHealth's earnings, and sees more than $2 a share of additional upside if those businesses improve further. His $455 target is 16.5 times his 2028 EPS estimate.

For Humana, TD Cowen forecasts 2028 adjusted EPS of $40.42, above the $37.81 consensus, and bases its $485 target on 12 times that figure. It noted Humana has cut some over-the-counter benefits by 47% and raised out-of-pocket limits for 2027.
The timing followed a sharp drop in insurers on 18 Nov when CMS proposed its so-called CRUSH rule to step up audits and recoup improper payments.
Walmart drew a broad round of target increases after results, with eight brokers lifting targets into a $135-$147 range.
detail.consensus: Brokers are leaning towards defensive health and staples names after the tech rout, though managed care still carries regulatory risk from the CMS proposal.
